A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same cue/reply watermarking framework for auditing LLM fine-tuning data. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including v1 Appendices A–C and v2 Appendices A–E.

before.justification: Section IV reports original LLaMA and Mistral fine-tuning experiments on Blog1k and Poems, measuring regurgitation, dataset-size sensitivity, multi-watermark interference, and ranking-test outcomes.

after.justification: Section 4 reports original fine-tuning experiments, including News and a competing watermarking method. Appendices D–E report individual-watermark analyses and character-preservation experiments.

M1.justification: The instantiated marking component changes from four specified invisible characters to a screened 121-character alphabet (Section 4.1 and Appendix E.1). The cue/reply construction, cyclic embedding, reply extraction, trusted attribution, and ranking algorithms remain substantively unchanged; moving Algorithms 1–3 into Appendix A and renaming cr to t do not introduce new procedures.

E1.justification: v2 adds CNN/DailyMail News, extending evaluation from blogs and poetry to longer news documents with multiple cue/reply chunks. Appendix E also adds distinct input-environment scenarios involving PDF viewers, websites, preprocessing pipelines, tokenizers, and chatbot interfaces. The six named cleaning pipelines are compatibility tests, not six additional fine-tuning datasets.

E2.justification: v1 discusses competing approaches without experimentally evaluating one. v2 Section 4.6 and Figure 5 evaluate Wei et al. (2024)'s homoglyph watermarking method under the 50-watermark setting across both models and all three datasets. Other approaches listed in Table 3 remain conceptual comparisons.

E3.justification: The multi-watermark experiment changes from 1,000 training documents and 4/8/12 watermarks to 5,000 documents and up to 50 watermarks. Its five-query document-success measure is replaced by single-query chunk-level regurgitation rates. v2 also changes the alphabet and sampled collections and introduces 200-word chunks for News. The LoRA, training, and generation settings in v1 Table IV and v2 Table 5 otherwise match.

E4.justification: Appendix E adds systematic character-preservation tests through PDF/web handling, six cleaning pipelines, ten tokenizers, and three chatbot interfaces, plus a tokenization comparison with emojis. v1 principally discussed these vulnerabilities and supplied a small ChatGPT example. The expanded multi-watermark sensitivity study and Appendix D also examine individual watermark trajectories and outliers.

E5.justification: v1 reports means and standard deviations over five verification runs. v2 reports 95% confidence intervals with aggregation over five watermarks and three prompts per chunk, and explicitly averages three ranking-test repetitions. The new baseline evaluation adds empirical Z-scores against 100 random sequences. These change statistical reporting and sampling structure; an increase in independent training seeds is not established.

E6.justification: The main numerical results are extensively replaced under revised settings. For example, Mistral/Poems at 50 marked documents has p=0.132 in v1 Table II and p=0.903 in v2 Table 1, with different alphabets and sampled documents. The ranking evaluation changes from reported 100% TPR with 18,810 counterfactual challenges to approximately 96.7% TPR with over 100,000, including a failed Mistral/News watermark. These are not matched-setting performance changes. News, baseline, and preservation results are newly reported.

T1.justification: v2 Section 3.1 and Appendix A.1 generalize v1's parameter-specific watermark-space calculation. They explicitly recognize overlap overcounting, treat the forbidden-cue count as an upper bound, and derive a lower bound on admissible watermarks. The ranking-test FPR bound and watermark-repetition derivation are retained.

C1.justification: The central contribution remains text-preserving, black-box provenance auditing with bounded false positives. v2 qualifies completeness around sufficiently large marked collections and limits robustness requirements to non-adversarial processing. Its abstract and conclusion replace v1's precise 100% TPR and failure-rate headlines with broader high-detection claims, while extending the stated marked-data fraction to 0.25%.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive qualifications about context-dependent invisibility, font/viewer dependence, chatbot filtering, and the distinction between excluding marked documents and erasing their marks. It interprets multiple watermarks as potentially strengthening memorization, whereas v1 emphasized mostly mild interference. Section 4.3 and Appendix D also introduce sampling and optimization noise as explanations for variability.

D1.justification: v2 newly identifies H100/H200 hardware and documents alphabet screening, pipeline reconstruction, tokenizer identifiers, PDF fonts/viewers, and chatbot test inputs. However, its exact expanded character list and several supporting artifacts are deferred until acceptance; v1 explicitly enumerated its four characters. v2 also qualifies the code-release claim with an acceptance-dependent release statement.

R1.justification: Related work is substantially refocused around provider-controlled watermarking versus data-owner provenance auditing and free-text generation. v2 adds discussions of Waterfall, DECOP, and WASA and introduces the capability comparison in Table 3. It removes the extensive lexical/syntactic/format-based taxonomy and associated discussions such as LexiMark, UniSpaCh, and Innamark.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, problem formulation, experimental narrative, and related work are substantially rewritten and condensed. Existing algorithms and notation move into Appendix A, the legal-context discussion moves into an Impact Statement, and related work now precedes limitations. These are extensive narrative and structural revisions beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: v2 changes the document template and appendix layout, redraws Figure 1, and reorganizes the main plots into dataset panels with rate axes. The multi-watermark boxplots become line plots with confidence bands, supplemented by individual-watermark curves. New baseline and tokenization figures, comparison and preservation tables, and expanded ranking-table columns substantially change the visual presentation.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's lack of an evaluated competitor and limited empirical support for practical robustness. The baseline comparison, longer-document evaluation, larger multi-watermark study, and Appendix E measurements strengthen the evidence while exposing deployment limitations. These gains outweigh remaining weaknesses: the expanded alphabet is not fully disclosed, and Section 4.2 overstates completeness by claiming miss probabilities below 0.01 for all 30-document settings when Table 1 reports 0.156 for Mistral/Blog1k.
